title: Node Pairs Whose Path Letters Can Mirror
statement:
A tree has n nodes numbered 0 to n − 1, rooted at node 0. It is given as parent, where parent[i] is the parent of node i and parent[0] = −1. The edge between node i and its parent carries the letter s[i]. The root has no such edge, so s[0] is ignored.

Count the pairs of nodes u < v such that the letters on the path between them can be rearranged into a palindrome.

examples.why: Edges: 0–1 a, 0–2 b, 1–3 b, 1–4 a. The path 0–1–4 reads "aa", fine. The path 3–1–4 reads "ba", which cannot be a palindrome; neither can 0–1–3 ("ab") or 1–0–2 ("ab"). The other 7 pairs work.
A chain of c's. Every path is all c's, so all 6 pairs work.
Root-to-child paths have one letter and work. Child-to-child paths have two different letters and do not.

constraints: parent[0] = −1, and parent describes a tree rooted at 0
hints: Letters can be rearranged into a palindrome exactly when at most one letter appears an odd number of times. Only the parity of each letter matters.

Store parities as a 26-bit mask and XOR as you walk. Let mask[v] be the XOR of the letters from the root down to v. The path u–v has mask mask[u] XOR mask[v], because the shared part above their meeting point cancels out.

So a pair works when mask[u] and mask[v] are equal or differ in one bit. Visit nodes one by one with a hash map of masks seen so far: add count[m] plus count[m ^ (1 << b)] for each of the 26 bits, then record m.

explain.intuition:
A bag of letters can be laid out as a palindrome when at most one letter has an odd count (it goes in the middle). So for each path you only need 26 bits of parity, and XOR flips a bit each time a letter appears.

The trick is to avoid walking paths at all. Give every node v the mask of the path from the root down to it. For two nodes, both root paths share the part above the point where they meet; XOR cancels that shared part, leaving exactly the mask of the u–v path. So the question becomes: how many earlier nodes have a mask equal to mine, or one bit away from mine? That is 27 hash lookups per node.
steps: Build the children lists from parent and walk the tree from the root (BFS or an explicit stack), setting mask[v] = mask[parent[v]] XOR (1 << letter s[v]) and mask[0] = 0.
Go through the nodes with a map count of masks seen so far.
For node with mask m, add count[m] (paths with all-even letters) and count[m ^ (1 << b)] for each b in 0..25 (one odd letter).
pitfalls: Using recursion on a tree that can be a 100 000-node chain: the call stack overflows. Walk iteratively.
Counting a pair twice by looking up all nodes instead of only earlier ones, or counting a node with itself.
Assuming parent[i] < i and filling masks in index order. Build the masks by walking down from the root.

solutions.title: Walk from every node
solutions.idea: From each node u, walk the whole tree carrying the parity mask of the path so far, and count nodes v > u where at most one bit is set.

solutions.title: Root masks and a hash map
solutions.idea: The path mask is mask[u] XOR mask[v]. Count earlier nodes whose mask equals the current one or differs in exactly one bit.

followups: Count only pairs whose path letters already read the same both ways, without rearranging. Why is that much harder?
Edges change their letters over time, with queries in between. Which part of the mask idea survives?
lcTitle: Count Paths That Can Form a Palindrome in a Tree
